evidence_quotes.quote: We study them using a stated preference experiment in Hangzhou, China, where households faced either an increasing block tariff (IBT) or a flat-rate tariff in the baseline scenario, followed by two hypothetical IBT schedules.

A one-standard-deviation increase in threshold tightness is associated with a 14.65 m3 reduction in annual household water consumption, about 14% of the sample mean; the price-gap estimate is smaller.
threshold tightness predicts willingness to adopt water-saving technologies, but not unfavorable bill assessments, and we find no clear visual evidence of marginal-price bunching.

raw_response.plain_vs_narrow_note: No divergence between narrow and plain Criterion 2 readings: nonlinear domestic water tariff design (increasing block tariffs vs. flat-rate tariffs, block quantity thresholds and price gaps) directly satisfies both the active 2026-10-13 narrow tariff/cost-recovery rule-type criterion and the literal/plain Criterion 2 wording. Both decisions are 'unsure' solely because full-text review is needed to determine whether Criterion 4 service-access/affordability outcomes (as opposed to purely hypothetical conservation demand-reduction and technology-adoption intentions) are substantively evaluated.
raw_response.rationale: This empirical study examines domestic water tariff structure (increasing block tariffs vs. flat-rate tariffs, focusing on block quantity threshold tightness and price gaps) among households in Hangzhou, China, satisfying Criterion 1 (household water service), Criterion 2 under both narrow and plain readings (tariff design), and Criterion 3 (empirical stated-preference and baseline household survey evidence). However, the study is framed around demand conservation and willingness to adopt water-saving technologies in hypothetical stated-preference IBT scenarios, while also reporting reductions in annual household water consumption and testing 'unfavorable bill assessments' (a plausible affordability/bill-burden indicator) alongside baseline IBT vs. flat-rate exposure. Full-text retrieval ('unsure') is required to verify whether the study reports eligible household water access, essential-quantity, or affordability outcomes rather than purely hypothetical behavioral conservation intentions.
